title: How Supply Chain Orchestration Helps Suppliers Prioritize Competing Retail Requests
summary: Supply chain orchestration for suppliers starts with ranking retailer requirements by cost of a miss, how long it stays hidden, and fix speed.
body_markdown:
In this article, learn about:


-


How retailer compliance requirements differ on timing, labeling, and fines


-


How to rank those requirements by what a miss costs, how long it stays hidden, and how fast it can be fixed


-


Why the on-time, in-full (OTIF) pass-or-fail line sets the floor for every ranking


-


How[electronic data interchange (EDI) connectivity](https://www.spscommerce.com/products/fulfillment/edi/) keeps each retailer’s current rules in one place


Every retailer a supplier sells to sends its own rulebook. Walmart fines a failed shipment 3% of the cost of goods on the cases that are missed, while Kroger charges $200 for any truck that arrives more than 30 minutes after its appointment. When a supplier only has one small team and has to meet both at the same time, that can cause chaos.


Supply chain orchestration, for a supplier in this position, means deciding which requirements get attention first. Below, we compare what five retailers ask for and then rank them.


## What Happens When Retailer Compliance Requirements Collide?


On paper, a supplier ships one product to many customers. In practice, what a supplier learned about one retailer’s shortage-claim process may not carry over to the next, and gaps often show up in the first quarter with a new retailer, when unexpected deductions arrive.


We’ve compiled the differences for five retailers below.


**Retailer**


**What it measures**


**Penalty**


Walmart


On-time: 90% for prepaid orders, 98% for collect orders ready for pickup. In-full: 95%.


3% of the cost of goods on the non-compliant cases, not the whole purchase order (PO)


Kroger


93% on time and 95% case fill


3% of the invoiced amount for a late PO, 3% of the missing items’ value for a short one, $200 per shipment more than 30 minutes past its appointment, and $500 per PO for labeling, case pack, or universal product code (UPC) errors


Target


At least 95% of the original PO quantities delivered, and an error-free advance ship notice (ASN) before the trailer’s in-yard time


A flat $0.75 per carton (minimum $100) for ASN and barcode errors, plus timing and quantity fines set as a percentage of cost of goods


UNFI


72 hours’ appointment notice at conventional centers and 24 hours at natural centers, with a 95% fill rate


$250 for arriving more than 30 minutes late, $500 for a no-show, and up to $500 per PO for missing or unreadable case barcodes


KeHE


Appointment requested at least seven days before the ship-to-arrive date, and 85% on time per quarter


$250 per late shipment in a quarter that misses the rate


Even where the rulebooks cover the same ground, they differ. Kroger’s late-delivery fine applies to the whole PO, Walmart’s applies only to the failed cases, and Kroger’s flat fees weigh more heavily on small orders.


**Related Reading:**[Retail Chargeback Costs: What Is a Compliance Cost Curve?](https://www.spscommerce.com/community/articles/retail-chargeback-costs-what-is-a-compliance-cost-curve)


## How Should a Supplier Rank Retailer Requirements?


Ranking requirements by retailer size is the obvious starting point. Revenue matters, but it’s only one of four inputs to consider.


Here’s how the four break down:


-


**Cost of a miss:** what the retailer’s penalty structure charges, whether that’s a flat fee per carton or a percentage of the PO.


-


**Revenue behind the account:** how much of the supplier’s business the retailer represents.


-


**Time to surface:** how long a problem stays hidden before a fine or deduction shows up.


-


**Speed of the fix:** how quickly a change can ship, such as a corrected label template compared with a new production schedule.


The headline number can mislead. As a hypothetical, a Target PO of 2,000 cartons with an ASN error would owe $1,500 (2,000 cartons at $0.75), while a labeling error at Kroger is a flat $500 per PO. The cheaper-looking fine becomes the expensive one as the order grows. Revenue share and fix effort come from your own data, so the inputs are weighed together, not run through a formula.


## Why Does the OTIF Scorecard Set the Floor?


A scorecard looks like a grade, but OTIF works as a pass or fail result for each order. A shipment that is 95% complete but on time still fails. OTIF is often calculated by multiplying the on-time rate by the in-full rate, so 90% on time and 95% in full gives a composite of 85.5% (0.90 x 0.95). That’s a common method, not a universal one, so it’s important to double-check each retailer’s definition.


The floor is the point where a retailer starts fining. At Walmart, that’s 90% on time for prepaid orders, 98% for collect orders ready for pickup, and 95% in full. Kroger sets 93% on time, and a supplier at 93% over a four-week period owes no late-arrival fees for that period. Ranking happens above those lines, and a requirement sitting below its line moves to the front regardless of revenue share.


New suppliers sometimes get room to work above the floor.


Walmart waives OTIF fines for a new supplier’s first three months while still tracking performance, and KeHE gives new brands a full year before penalty fees begin.


**Related Reading:**[A Realistic Scorecard Timeline for a New Supplier’s First 6 Months](https://www.spscommerce.com/community/articles/a-realistic-scorecard-timeline-for-a-new-suppliers-first-6-months)


## How Does Detection Lag Change the Ranking?


A fine doesn’t arrive with the shipment that caused it.


Walmart generally issues fines quarterly, about five weeks after the quarter ends. A miss in a quarter’s last week surfaces about five weeks later, while a miss in its first week waits a full quarter plus those five weeks.


Dispute windows differ too. Kroger allows 180 days from the original invoice date for billing inquiries, and Target’s window is generally three months. A repeated miss keeps costing money until the first fine appears, so a problem that surfaces slowly can deserve attention ahead of one that surfaces at once, even when its cost per miss is lower.


**Related Reading:**[Retailer Deductions in Q4: How Walmart and Kroger Compare](https://www.spscommerce.com/community/articles/retailer-deductions-in-q4-how-walmart-and-kroger-compare)


## Where Do Different Retailers’ Rules Overlap?


Several retailers check the same things at the dock, so one fix can clear more than one rulebook. Labeling is the clearest case. Kroger charges $500 per PO for case labeling, case pack, or UPC errors, Target fines $0.75 per carton for barcode errors, and UNFI charges up to $500 per PO for unreadable case barcodes. Appointment timing works the same way. Kroger charges $200 and UNFI charges $250 when a truck arrives more than 30 minutes after its appointment, so a change to how carriers are scheduled helps with both.


Item data causes some of the same problems. In 2026, Target added an audit in which distribution centers compare an item’s dimensions and weights to the item record, so a wrong number in the record can lead to a problem when the shipment arrives. The SPS scorecard guide says OTIF and fill rate failures are almost always symptoms of a problem that started earlier, such as inventory accuracy, ASN timing, or production scheduling.


Finding the cause is often the hard part. Lifetime Brands, a housewares company with more than 20 brands, couldn’t tell which distribution center was behind its non-compliant shipments. After drilling into its scorecard data, it moved from an F to an A+ with its largest U.S. retailer over about two and a half years.


## Who Should Own Each Retailer?


One approach is to give each retailer a single owner and a dated record of what changed and when. The dates matter because windows and channels differ: Amazon disputes run through Vendor Central, Target’s through a supplier portal, and Walmart’s through Retail Link. A dated record shows which deductions are still open.


## Frequently Asked Questions


### Which retailer requirement should a small supplier fix first?


The starting point is any requirement sitting below a retailer’s fining line, followed by fixes that clear several rulebooks at once, such as label accuracy and appointment timing.


### Do new suppliers pay fines right away?


Not always. Walmart waives OTIF fines for three months and KeHE gives new brands a full year, while other retailers set their own terms, so it’s important to check each one.


### What is the difference between a fine and a deduction?


A fine is a penalty invoice for a specific infraction, and a deduction is the retailer paying less than the supplier invoiced. Retailers sometimes use the terms interchangeably.
